questions.question: What is a lambda expression in Java and why was it introduced?
questions.title: Lambda Expressions in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A lambda expression is a short, unnamed function you can pass around as a value. Introduced in Java 8, it replaces verbose anonymous classes and powers the Streams API. Lambdas only work with functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands lambdas as a language feature and the motivation behind Java 8's functional additions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing lambda syntax without explaining functional interfaces — the type a lambda actually targets
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect lambdas to the Streams API and mention method references as the even-shorter form

sections.title: What a Lambda Expression Is
sections.content:
A **lambda expression** is a short block of code you can pass around like a value — a function with no name. You write the parameters, then `->`, then the body, and that's it.

Why it exists: before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an **anonymous class** — five lines of wrapper for one line of real logic. A lambda trims that wrapper away so only the logic is left.

How it works: a lambda is not a free-floating function. It targets a **functional interface** — an interface with exactly one abstract method — and becomes the body of that single method. The compiler infers the parameter types from that target, so you skip writing them.

Lambdas come in a few shapes:
- `() -> expr` — no parameters
- `s -> s.length() > 5` — one parameter, parentheses optional
- `(a, b) -> a + b` — two parameters

They are also what powers the Streams API: `filter`, `map`, and `sorted` all take lambdas.

> **The gotcha:** a lambda only works where a single-abstract-method interface is expected — point it at a regular class and it won't compile.

sections.title: Lambda at a Glance
How a Lambda Binds to a Functional Interface
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB L["Lambda
(a, b) becomes a.compareTo(b)"] --> T["Target type
a functional interface"] T --> M["Single abstract method
e.g. Comparator.compare"] L --> I["Compiler infers
the parameter types"] M --> R["Lambda becomes
that method's body"] ``` The lambda has no type of its own — it borrows the shape of whichever single-method interface is expected at that spot.

sections.title: Before lambdas vs after
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the functional interface**: Freshers describe lambda syntax but can't name what type a lambda becomes. A lambda needs a target interface with exactly one abstract method, like `Runnable` or `Comparator` — without one, it won't compile.
- **Treating a lambda as a standalone function**: Trying to call a lambda where a plain method is expected. A lambda only fits where a functional-interface type is the expected target, not as a free function.
- **Overusing block bodies**: Wrapping a single expression in `{ return ...; }` braces. Prefer `x -> x * 2` over `x -> { return x * 2; }` when the body is one expression.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Lambda = anonymous function** — has parameters, body, return type — but no name
- **Only works with functional interfaces** — interfaces with exactly one abstract method
- **Syntax:** `(params) -> expression` or `(params) -> { statements; }`
- **Type inference:** the compiler figures out parameter types from context — you don't declare them
- **Powers the Streams API** — filter, map, sort all take lambdas as arguments
- **Method references** (`String::compareTo`) are an even shorter form when the lambda just calls an existing method

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
A lambda expression is a short, unnamed function that you can pass around as a value.

Before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an anonymous class — 5-6 lines for what is conceptually one line of logic. A custom sort comparator needed a full Comparator class definition.

With lambdas, you write just the logic — like (a, b) arrow a.compareTo(b). Same result, one line.

Why was it introduced? Java 8 added the Streams API for processing collections. Streams need you to pass functions — filter items where length is greater than five, transform each item to uppercase. Without lambdas, every step would need an anonymous class, making streams unreadable. Lambdas make it clean.

One rule to remember: lambdas only work with functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method. The lambda provides the implementation of that one method.

questions.question: What is 'effectively final' and why do lambdas require it?
questions.title: Effectively Final Variables in Lambdas
questions.direct_answer: 'Effectively final' means a local variable is assigned once and never reassigned. Lambdas can only capture local variables that are final or effectively final, because the captured value must stay stable even if the lambda runs later on another thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of variable capture and why the JVM enforces the effectively-final rule
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying the variable must be declared final — effectively final means the compiler infers it, no keyword needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the stack-vs-heap lifetime reason and mention the single-element-array workaround as a code smell

sections.title: What 'Effectively Final' Means
sections.content:
**Effectively final** means a local variable is assigned once and then never changed again. Java added the idea in Java 8 so you don't have to spell out the `final` keyword everywhere.

Why lambdas care: a lambda can capture local variables from the method around it, but only if they are final or effectively final. The reason is **lifetime**. Local variables live on the stack and vanish when the method returns, yet a lambda can be stored and run much later — maybe on another thread. So the lambda captures a stable copy of the value.

How the compiler decides: it simply checks whether you ever reassign the variable after its first value.
- Assign once, never touch it again → effectively final → the lambda compiles.
- Reassign it even once → not effectively final → compile error.

That is why `count++` or `name = "new"` after the first assignment breaks capture.

> **The gotcha:** the rule is about reassignment, not mutation — a captured `List` can still have items added to it.

sections.title: Capture Rules at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Effectively final|~assigned exactly once|never reassigned|no `final` keyword needed|compiler infers it
blue|Why the rule exists|~locals live on the stack|lambda may run later / on another thread|needs a stable captured value|a changing value would be stale
emerald|What breaks it|~count++|name = "new"|any reassignment after init|then the lambda won't compile

sections.title: When Capture Compiles and When It Breaks
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Local variable
assigned a value"] --> B{"Reassigned
later?"} B -- No --> C["Effectively final
lambda captures a copy"] B -- Yes --> D["Not effectively final
compile error"] C --> E["Lambda can run later
the value stays stable"] ``` The single question the compiler asks is whether the variable is ever reassigned — everything else follows from that.

sections.title: Effectively final — what works and what doesn't
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking you must write `final`**: Believing the variable needs the `final` keyword. Effectively final means the compiler infers it — no keyword is needed as long as you never reassign.
- **Reassigning a captured variable**: Updating a counter or accumulator like `total += x` in the surrounding method, then wondering why the lambda no longer compiles.
- **Reaching for the array hack**: Using a single-element array `int[] c = {0}` to fake a mutable counter inside a lambda. It compiles, but it's a code smell and is unsafe across threads.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Effectively final** — assigned once, never reassigned; no `final` keyword required
- **Applies to local variables only** — instance and static fields are exempt
- **Why:** a lambda may outlive its method (run later or on another thread) so it needs a stable captured value
- **What breaks it:** any reassignment such as `count++` or `name = ...` after initialization
- **Reassignment, not mutation:** a captured `List` can still be modified; you just can't point the variable at a new object
- **Workaround:** a single-element array holds mutable state — but it's a code smell and unsafe across threads

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
When a lambda captures a local variable from the surrounding method, that variable must be effectively final — meaning it's assigned once and never changed.

Why does this rule exist? A lambda can be stored and run later — maybe on a different thread, after the original method has returned. Local variables live on the stack and disappear when the method exits. The lambda needs a stable copy of the value. If the variable could change, the copy would be stale and misleading.

Effectively final means you don't have to write the final keyword — the compiler just checks that you never reassign the variable. If you write count equals five or count plus plus anywhere after the initial assignment, the variable is no longer effectively final and the lambda using it won't compile.

Instance and static variables don't have this restriction — they're on the heap and stay alive as long as the object exists.

questions.question: Can a lambda expression access instance variables and static variables?
questions.title: Variable Access Inside Lambdas
questions.direct_answer: Yes. The effectively-final restriction applies only to local variables. Instance and static variables live on the heap, so a lambda can both read and write them freely. Inside a lambda, 'this' refers to the enclosing class instance, not the lambda itself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of which variable kinds a lambda can mutate and how 'this' behaves inside a lambda
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming instance fields have the same effectively-final restriction as local variables
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast lambda 'this' with anonymous-class 'this' — lambdas have no identity of their own

sections.title: Lambda Variable Access
sections.content:
Inside a lambda you can use variables from the surrounding code, but what you're allowed to do depends on the **kind of variable**. Local variables are read-only; instance and static variables can be read and written.

Why the split: it comes down to where the data lives. A **local variable** sits on the stack and disappears when the method returns, so the lambda only gets a frozen, effectively-final copy. An **instance variable** (a field) or a `static` variable lives on the heap and stays alive with the object or class, so the lambda can change it freely.

A quick summary of the three kinds:
- Local variable → read-only, must be effectively final.
- Instance field → full read and write.
- `static` field → full read and write.

One more detail interviewers like: inside a lambda the `this` keyword refers to the **enclosing class instance**, not the lambda. A lambda has no identity of its own.

> **The gotcha:** an anonymous class has its own `this`, but a lambda borrows the outer one — so `this.field` reaches the surrounding object.

sections.title: Access by Variable Kind
sections.content:
amber|Local variable|~read-only inside a lambda|must be effectively final|lives on the stack|needs a stable copy
blue|Instance + static|~full read AND write access|no restriction|live on the heap|stay alive with the object/class
emerald|`this` keyword|~refers to enclosing instance|NOT the lambda|differs from anonymous classes|lambdas have no own identity

sections.title: What a Lambda Can Do per Variable Kind
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Variable used
inside a lambda"] --> B{"Which kind?"} B -- Local --> C["Read-only
must be effectively final"] B -- Instance field --> D["Read and write
lives on the heap"] B -- Static field --> E["Read and write
lives on the heap"] ``` The deciding factor is always memory: stack-bound locals are frozen, while heap-bound fields are fully writable.

sections.title: Lambda variable access — all three types
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming fields need effectively final too**: Freshers think instance variables follow the same rule as locals. Fields live on the heap, so a lambda can reassign them freely.
- **Misreading `this`**: Expecting `this` inside a lambda to point at the lambda object. It points at the enclosing instance — unlike an anonymous class, which has its own `this`.
- **Mutating shared fields without care**: Writing to an instance or `static` field from a lambda that runs on another thread, creating a race condition with no synchronization.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Local variables** — read-only inside a lambda, and must be effectively final
- **Instance variables** — full read/write access, no restriction (heap-resident)
- **Static variables** — full read/write access, same heap reasoning
- **`this` in a lambda** — refers to the enclosing class instance, not the lambda
- **Contrast:** anonymous classes have their own `this`; lambdas do not
- **Thread caution:** writing shared fields from a lambda on another thread still needs synchronization

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
It depends on what type of variable.

Local variables are read-only inside a lambda, and only if they're effectively final. They live on the stack and the lambda needs a stable copy.

Instance variables — the fields of the class — get full read and write access, with no restriction. They live on the heap and won't disappear.

Static variables also get full read and write access. Same reason — they're on the heap for the class's lifetime.

One important detail about the this keyword: inside a lambda, this refers to the enclosing class instance, not the lambda. This is different from anonymous classes, where this refers to the anonymous class itself. Lambdas don't have their own identity — they're just behaviour, not objects.
